name: Aguaruna
confidence_why: Overall 2007, Corbera Mori 1994 and Payne 1990 all describe Aguaruna as a pitch accent language with one culminative high-pitched accent per word that is partly lexical, and the ILV descriptions by Fast and Larson 1974 and Jakway, Antunce and Wipio 1996 mark one contrastive accent per word in the same way, differing only on whether a default second-mora position for nouns can be stated.

catalog_quote: Aguaruna has a pitch accent: in every phonological word, one syllable carries an accent, and is pronounced with a higher pitch than the rest of the word. The principle of “one word per accent, one accent per word” is an important criterion and diagnostic of wordhood (§2.8). Perhaps the most interesting feature of accent assignment is that it operates differently in verbs and nouns (with adjectives following the nominal pattern) ... • Some, but not all, verbal roots and suffixes have lexically specified accents; only the leftmost accent surfaces in the verbal word and if there is no underlying accent a default rule applies. • Nouns and adjectives may have lexically specified accents, but there is little evidence that nominal suffixes do. Instead, most nominal suffixes trigger accent shift in the root. ... Accent is potentially phonemically contrastive, and surface minimal pairs can readi…
sweep_summary: Aguaruna (agua1253) is in the catalog as 'tonal' (culminative pitch accent) on Overall 2007 §2.7. The four title-keyword items are three works by David L. Payne — 1978 SIL-Peru microfiche 'Aguaruna pitch accent' (IC 373e; not online), 1989 'Extrametricalidad y acento tonal en el aguaruna' (Temas de lingüística amerindia, pp. 251-272; no open copy found), and 1990 'Accent in Aguaruna' (Amazonian Linguistics pp. 161-184; DOI 10.7560/704145-008, De Gruyter/UT Press paywalled, HathiTrust search-only) — plus Glottolog 639096, a Glossa-derived duplicate that mis-cites the 1990 chapter as Payne & Payne pp. 185-212. None could be downloaded open; sil. Payne's rule was nevertheless read at second hand: Overall 2007 fn.44 (p.108) quotes Payne 1990b:180 verbatim (default high pitch on the second mora from the left in substantives, lexical exceptions on the first or third mora), and Corbera Mori 1994 §2.4 (held by the project, pp. 43-50) summarises the same analysis (never final mora; bimoraic words initial; extrametricality; seven suffix classes) and calls Aguaruna a pitch accent language with one main accent per word realised as high tone, while doubting full predictability. Both refine but do not contradict the catalog: pitch accent coding stands; a mora-counting default exists in Payne's analysis. Best new statement = the Payne 1990b:180 sentence via Overall fn.44; it does not supersede Overall 2007. Acquire Payne 1990 (high) and Payne 1989 (high, Spanish version); Payne 1978 low; 639096 merge with 73356. Records with.

new_statements.quote: “[T]he basic pattern of accent assignment on Aguaruna substantives assigns high pitch to the second mora from the beginning of the word. Certain exceptions have lexically marked accents on the first or third moras.”
new_statements.citation: Payne, David L. 1990. Accent in Aguaruna. In Doris L. Payne (ed.), Amazonian linguistics: Studies in lowland South American languages, 161-184. Austin: University of Texas Press, p. 180 — read as the verbatim quotation in Overall, Simon E. 2007, A Grammar of Aguaruna, PhD thesis, La Trobe University, p. 108 fn. 44 (p. 131); corroborated by Corbera Mori 1994 §2.4 pp. 44-47.
new_statements.locator: Payne 1990b: 180, quoted in Overall 2007 p.108 fn.44; Corbera 1994 pp. 44-47
new_statements.reading: Payne's own statement of the rule: Aguaruna nouns and adjectives have a culminative pitch accent (high pitch) whose default position is the second mora (= second vowel) from the left edge of the word; first- or third-mora accent is lexically marked (Corbera's summary adds: never on the final mora, bimoraic words on the first mora, some exceptions handled by extrametricality). This is a pitch accent system with a left-edge mora-counting default plus lexical exceptions, so the catalog's 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent) coding stands; the refinement is that a default position rule exists in Payne's analysis (second mora from the left in substantives), which Overall 2007 acknowledges in fn.44 while judging nominal accent not predictable enough to state a rule. Caveat: the Payne sentence was read as a verbatim quotation transmitted by Overall, not from the chapter itself (paywalled DOI 10.7560/704145-008).

new_statements.quote: Aunque se indica el acento con acento ortográfico en todas las palabras en el diccionario para ayudar con la pronunciación, por lo general no se escribe en el alfabeto práctico [text layer reads 'pnictico']. El acento ortográfico se escribe en casos de formas homófonas, en las palabras cuya sílaba final termina en vocal acentuada y en palabras de origen castellano. Por razones ortográficas no se escribe la nasalización vocálica aunque resultan algunas formas homófonas. Ejs.: ayát "salar" y ayát (pronunciado con nasalización en la segunda sílaba) "llevar; llevar consigo".
new_statements.translation: Although the accent is indicated with an orthographic accent on all words in the dictionary to help with pronunciation, it is generally not written in the practical alphabet. The orthographic accent is written in cases of homophonous forms, in words whose final syllable ends in an accented vowel, and in words of Spanish origin. For orthographic reasons vowel nasalization is not written, although some homophonous forms result. E.g. ayát 'to salt' and ayát (pronounced with nasalization on the second syllable) 'to carry; to take along'.
new_statements.citation: Jakway, Martha A. and Antunce S., Alejandro Paati and Wipio D., Gerardo (1996). Diccionario aguaruna- castellano, castellano- aguaruna. Lima: Ministerio de Educación and Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 296 pp.

The whole paragraph is verbatim at p.14 = printed p.16 'ALFABETO' in lines 396-402), including the scanned form 'pnictico' the compiler flagged; it is the last paragraph before Parte I, after the notes on voiceless vowels 'en algunas areas' and double vowels. 'refines' is defensible but thin: the paragraph is an orthographic note (accent written on every headword to aid pronunciation; practical alphabet writes it only for homophones, words ending in an accented vowel, Spani…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's pitch accent reading (Payne 1990: default high pitch on the second mora from the left, lexical exceptions, no stems accented on the final mora): the dictionary confirms a single culminative accent per word and treats final-vowel accent as marked/exceptional; it does not itself state the second-mora default and does not call the accent pitch.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated. The dictionary marks one accent on every headword (e.g. ápa 'padre', dúku 'madre', kánu 'canoa', pagáat(a) 'caña de azúcar', pabáu 'tapir', takát 'trabajo', aagkú 'tarde'), so word accent is culminative and treated as a property of each word; the practical orthography writes it only where it is not recoverable (homophones, words with an accented final vowel, Spanish loans).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; one accent per headword.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with an accented final vowel are singled out as needing the written accent in the practical alphabet, i.e. treated as the non-default case; Spanish loans keep their own accent.
new_statements.identity_note: All works are on Aguaruna proper (Peru, Amazonas/Marañón area ILV materials). Fast & Larson 1974 (introduction) note several dialects differing in pronunciation (e.g. voiceless final vowels audible in one dialect) and say those differences are ignored; the dictionary likewise notes voiceless vowels 'en algunas áreas'. No source assigns its accent statements to a specific dialect.

new_statements.quote: Si no cae sobre una mayúscula, el acento se marca en cada palabra con más de una sílaba. El sentido de la palabra varía a veces según el acento. núgka "tierra" nugká "abajo" o "en la tierra" || p.29: Si el radical tiene solamente dos sílabas no hay ninguna letra que desaparece, sólo el acento cambia. En todas palabras, el acento pasa a la próxima sílaba de la izquierda con la excepción de las palabras que sostienen la tercera sílaba por tener un grupo de consonantes heterogéneas entre las dos últimas sílabas.
new_statements.translation: Unless it would fall on a capital letter, the accent is marked on every word of more than one syllable. The meaning of the word sometimes varies according to the accent. núgka 'earth' / nugká 'below' or 'on the earth' || p.29: If the root has only two syllables no letter disappears, only the accent changes. In all words the accent moves to the next syllable to the left, except in words that keep the third syllable because they have a heterogeneous consonant cluster between the last two syllables.

En todas palabras, el acento pasa a la proxima silaba de la izquierda con la excepcion de las palabras que sostienen la tercera silaba por tener un grupo de consonantes heterogene…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's pitch accent reading (Payne 1990: default on the second mora from the left, lexical exceptions, no stems accented on the final mora). The observed leftward shift when a final vowel is lost is what a mora-counting-from-the-left rule with final extrametricality predicts, and the final-accented locative/vocative forms are suffixal accents on inflected words, not stems, so they do not contradict Payne's 'no stems accented on the final mora'. It differs only in framing: Fast & Larson mark accent per word and state no default position.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A pedagogical grammar: it gives no placement rule, marks the accent on every polysyllabic word for the learner, and shows that accent position can distinguish forms (núgka 'tierra' vs nugká 'en la tierra'). It adds three morphophonological facts: (a) p.18, the locative is 'la vocal nasalizada con acento', i.e. an accented final nasal vowel (jeegá 'en la casa' vs jeegánum 'dentro de la casa'; nugká vs nugkánum); (b) p.29, when the root-final vowel is dropped to form the subject (nominative) form, the accent moves one syllable to the left (yugkumá- > yugkám, kutagká- > kutág, pisháka- > píshak), except where a heterogeneous cluster keeps the third syllable; (c) p.66, the vocative of proper names ending in a vowel is formed 'poniendo el acento en la última sílaba' (Pítja > Pitjá), and kin vocatives take accented -á/-í/-wá/-tá. The 'lexical' reading is the source's implicit stance (accent must be learned per word); it does not call the accent pitch and does not give Payne's second-mora default.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; one accent per word.
new_statements.exceptions: Vocative suffixes and proper-name vocatives carry final accent (p.66); locative is an accented final nasalized vowel (p.18); leftward accent shift under final-vowel loss in subject forms, blocked when a heterogeneous cluster sustains the third syllable (p.29); the introduction notes dialects differing in pronunciation (voiceless final vowels in one dialect) but assigns no dialect to the accent statements.
new_statements.identity_note: All works are on Aguaruna proper (Peru, Amazonas/Marañón area ILV materials). Fast & Larson 1974 (introduction) note several dialects differing in pronunciation (e.g. voiceless final vowels audible in one dialect) and say those differences are ignored; the dictionary likewise notes voiceless vowels 'en algunas áreas'. No source assigns its accent statements to a specific dialect.

readall_conflicts: No source opened contradicts the catalog's pitch accent reading (Payne 1990 via Overall 2007 and Corbera Mori 1994: culminative high pitch, default on the second mora from the left, lexical first/third-mora accents, extrametricality, no stems accented on the final mora). The two ILV sources that say anything (Fast & Larson 1974; Jakway et al. 1996) do not state a default position and do not call the accent 'pitch': they mark one accent on every word and treat final-vowel accent as the case needing written marking. Fast & Larson's final-accented locatives (nugká) and vocatives (Pitjá) and the dictionary's final-accented headwords such as aagkú 'tarde' are word-level accents on inflected or suffixed forms and do not conflict with Payne's stem-level claim, though a reader restricting Payne's rule to whole words would see a tension. Fast & Larson's leftward accent shift under final-vowel loss (p.29) is the kind of alternation Payne's mora-counting analysis was built to explain, so it corroborates rather than conflicts. Payne 1989 (the Spanish treatment) could not be opened and Payne 1976 was read only in excerpt; Larson 1963 and 1978 are silent.

sources.quote: p.44 (PDF 54): 'O Aguaruna parece ser uma língua de acento tonal (pitch accent), ou seja, uma língua em que cada palavra leva um acento principal e sem acentos secundários. A manifestação fonética do acento principal é o tom alto.' Cites Pike & Larson (1964:64) that accent placement is 'lexically-controlled' and lists minimal pairs (Sikít 'urinar' / Síkít 'levar agua', túntu / tuntú); then summarizes Payne (1990): accent never on the final mora; 'o acento em Aguaruna é considerado por Payne como previsível, e ocorre normalmente na segunda mora da palavra, contando a partir da margem esquerda.
sources.note: Second full grammar in Glottolog's list; §2.4 gives an independent pitch accent statement and a suffix-class accent-shift summary. downloaded now; confirms the classification.
